hints: Notice the question gives a constant resultant force $F$ acting for a time $t$ and asks for change in momentum $\Delta p$.
Connect this to Newton's second law in momentum form where force equals rate of change of momentum, $F = \Delta p / t$.
Rearrange to make $\Delta p$ the subject by multiplying both sides by the time $t$ and check that $Ft$ has momentum units of $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Identify the useful givens: resultant force $F$, time interval $t$, and required quantity change in momentum $\Delta p$.
State the governing rule: Newton's second law as $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$ for a constant resultant force.
Rearrange by multiplying by time: $\Delta p = F \times t$.
Check units: $F$ in $\text{N}$ times $t$ in $\text{s}$ gives $\text{N s}$, which is identical to $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$ for momentum.
Mass $m$ is not needed separately because $F$ already accounts for the acceleration of that mass.

options.A: Dividing $F$ by $t$ gives units of $\text{N s}^{-1}$, not momentum, and does not represent impulse.
options.B: This is $Ft$ divided by $m$, which equals change in velocity $\Delta v$, not change in momentum.
options.C: Impulse equals change in momentum, so $\Delta p = Ft$ for constant resultant force $F$ acting for time $t$.
options.D: Dividing $F$ by $mt$ gives units of $\text{s}^{-2}$ times length, which cannot equal momentum.
